newsitem.title: UK: Weak Wall Street depresses European bourses.
newsitem.headline: Weak Wall Street depresses European bourses.

text.p: Leading European stock markets slipped to their lowest levels of a lacklustre day on Tuesday after profit-taking pushed down Wall Street by half a percent at its opening.
Bourses had earlier been mixed or lower in thin trade, nervously expecting Wall Street to cash in on gains after its record closing high on Monday.
Market sentiment was further weighed down by continuing worries about interest rate hikes.
On the currency markets, the dollar edged lower, trading around 1.56 marks and above 115 yen but remaining in narrow ranges.

Dealers said underlying bullish dollar sentiment was intact, though the U.S. currency had slipped from 45-month highs of 117 yen on Monday after Japanese officials again warned against excessive yen weakness.
In London, Europe's busiest stock exchange, shares opened down and fell to their lowest levels, more than half a percent off, after New York's opening.

Sentiment was affected not only by weaker New York stocks but by a scarcity of corporate news and concern that credit might soon be tightened in the United States and in Britain -- which would make equities relatively less attractive to investors.
"People are expecting (British) rates to go up sometime this quarter but until the rate picture becomes clear, the uncertainty will remain and dog the market," one dealer commented.
Analysts still expect the London share market to test its all-time highs in coming weeks but the spectre of higher interest rates should limit the upside.

"The FTSE's uptrend is still intact and it could test new highs in the near term," said Kirit Shah, strategist at Sanwa International. "But with the bond market already factoring in a U.S. rate hike, the market will remain volatile."

In Frankfurt, German shares recovered morning losses to end afternoon bourse trade slightly up but they slid in electronic trading after the New York opening. By 1530 GMT the IBIS DAX index was down nearly half a percent.
German stocks were unmoved by news of industrial orders rising an expected 0.5 percent in November compared to October.
It was a similar story in Paris, where blue chips managed to show a small gain ahead of Wall Street but then, hampered by falling bond prices, followed the Dow into negative territory.

Both equity and currency traders said markets were nervous ahead of key U.S. statistics due out later in the week -- Thursday's producer price index and Friday's non-farm payrolls -- which will give clues to future movements of U.S. interest rates.

In currencies, the yen's partial recovery came after comments from Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka, who said: "An excessively weak or strong yen is not favourable for the Japanese economy. We want exchange rates to stabilise."
Analysts regarded the comments as pre-emptive strikes against a quickly falling yen but they said it was unlikely Tokyo would take action to strengthen the currency.
The comeback by the yen did little to boost Tokyo stocks and the Nikkei average fell a sharp 2.83 percent to its lowest close in more than a year on deepening concern about Japan's economy.
The dollar also slipped against the mark after Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer was quoted as saying he saw no need for German interest rate policy to change for the time being.
CURRENCIES AT 1530 GMT
The dollar was quoted around 1.5630 marks and 115.35 yen compared with 1.5665 and 115.60 in late European trade on Monday.
STOCK MARKETS AT 1530 GMT
The FTSE 100 index of key British shares was 22.6 points lower at 4,083.9.
The 30-share DAX index in Frankfurt closed 4.81 points up at 2,886.13 and the IBIS DAX index was down 11.74 at 2,878.46. In Paris, the CAC-40 index was down 1.22 at 2,305.39.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold fixed at $359.00 in the afternoon, up slightly from London's Monday close of $357.95. Silver was also stronger at $4.72.
